course.title: HTTP & REST
course.description: Speak the web's protocol fluently: requests and responses, method semantics, status codes, headers, URLs, and the REST conventions every JSON API is built on.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Request & Response
lessons.explanation:
## What actually goes over the wire

Every HTTP exchange is two messages. The client sends a **request**; the server answers with a **response**. Strip away the networking and each one is startlingly simple.

A request has four parts:

- **method** — the verb: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, ...
- **path** — which resource: `/users/42`
- **headers** — key/value metadata: `content-type: application/json`
- **body** — the payload (often absent; `GET` requests normally have none)

A response has three: a **status code** (`200`, `404`, ...), **headers**, and a **body**.

In this course we model requests as plain JavaScript objects so every exercise is a pure function — no network needed:

```js
const req = {
  method: 'POST',
  path: '/users',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: { name: 'Ada' },
};
```

Line by line: `method` is always stored **uppercase** by convention. `path` starts with `/`. Header names are stored **lowercase** — HTTP header names are case-insensitive (`Content-Type` and `content-type` are the same header), and lowercasing on the way in means you can look them up with plain property access. `body` holds the parsed payload, or `null` when there is none.

### Common mistakes

- Treating header names as case-sensitive. `req.headers['Content-Type']` misses `'content-type'` — normalize to lowercase once, at the edge.
- Assuming every request has a body. `GET` and `DELETE` usually don't; always handle `body: null`.

lessons.title: Methods: Safety & Idempotency
lessons.explanation:
## Five verbs, two properties

REST APIs lean on five methods, and two properties of each method matter more than anything else:

- **Safe** — the request changes nothing on the server. You can fire it a million times and the data is identical. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` are safe.
- **Idempotent** — doing it **twice leaves the server in the same state as doing it once**. All safe methods are idempotent, and so are `PUT` and `DELETE`. `POST` and `PATCH` are not guaranteed to be.

| method | meaning | safe | idempotent |
|--------|---------|------|------------|
| GET    | read a resource          | yes | yes |
| POST   | create / do a thing      | no  | **no** |
| PUT    | replace a resource whole | no  | yes |
| PATCH  | modify part of it        | no  | no |
| DELETE | remove it                | no  | yes |

### Worked example: why idempotency pays your salary

```js
// PUT /users/42  { name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }   — run twice: user 42 is... the same
// DELETE /users/42                                 — run twice: user 42 is... still gone
// POST /orders   { item: 'coffee' }                — run twice: TWO orders. Oops.
```

Line by line: `PUT` sends the **entire new state**, so repeating it just rewrites the same state. `DELETE` twice: the second call finds nothing to delete (it may answer 404), but the *server state* is identical — that is all idempotency promises. `POST` twice creates two resources: this is why a flaky network + an automatic retry on POST double-charges credit cards, and why payment APIs demand idempotency keys.

### Common mistakes

- Thinking idempotent means "same response every time". It means same *server state* — the second DELETE may return 404 instead of 204 and still be idempotent.
- Using GET for anything that mutates. Crawlers, prefetchers, and retries all assume GET is harmless.

lessons.title: Status Codes
Headers, Content Types & Auth
lessons.explanation:
## Metadata that makes the web work

Headers are where requests and responses describe *themselves*. Four you will touch daily:

- **Content-Type** — "here is what MY body is": `application/json; charset=utf-8`. Sent by whoever is sending a body.
- **Accept** — "here is what I can digest": the client's wish list for the RESPONSE body, e.g. `application/json, text/html`.
- **Authorization** — credentials. The dominant scheme is Bearer tokens: `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...` — the word `Bearer`, one space, the token.
- **Cache-Control** — caching rules as comma-separated directives: `max-age=60, no-cache` (some are flags, some have `=value`).

### Worked example: pulling a Bearer token apart

```js
const value = 'Bearer abc123';
const [scheme, token] = value.split(' ');
if (scheme === 'Bearer' && token) {
  // token === 'abc123' — look it up, find the user
}
```

Line by line: the header value is `scheme SP credentials`. Splitting on the space gives both halves; you must check the scheme really is `Bearer` (a `Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz` header would otherwise slip through) and that a token actually followed. Every auth middleware you will ever write starts with these four lines.

### Common mistakes

- Comparing content types with `===` and getting burned by `'; charset=utf-8'` suffixes — match the media type prefix.
- Forgetting Content-Type describes *the body it travels with*, while Accept is a wish about *the other party's reply*.

lessons.title: URLs & Query Strings
lessons.explanation:
## Taking a URL apart without regex

Node (and every browser) ships two classes that make URL handling a solved problem — never parse URLs with string hacking:

```js
const u = new URL('https://api.shop.io:8080/products/42?color=red&page=2#reviews');
u.protocol   // 'https:'
u.hostname   // 'api.shop.io'
u.port       // '8080'
u.pathname   // '/products/42'
u.search     // '?color=red&page=2'
u.hash       // '#reviews'
u.searchParams.get('page')   // '2'   ← a STRING, always
```

Line by line: the constructor validates and splits the URL once; every component is then a property. The big one is `searchParams` — a `URLSearchParams` object with `get`, `getAll`, `set`, `append`, and `toString()`. Two facts to tattoo somewhere:

1. **Every query value is a string.** `?page=2` gives you `'2'`, not `2`. Parse and validate before doing math.
2. `URLSearchParams` handles **encoding** for you: `set('q', 'coffee mug')` serializes as `q=coffee+mug`, and `get` decodes it back. Hand-building query strings with `+` concatenation is how you get broken links and injection bugs.

### Worked example: pagination with guardrails

```js
const params = new URLSearchParams('page=3&perPage=500');
let page = Number.parseInt(params.get('page') ?? '', 10);
if (Number.isNaN(page) || page < 1) page = 1;        // default & floor
let perPage = Number.parseInt(params.get('perPage') ?? '', 10);
if (Number.isNaN(perPage) || perPage < 1) perPage = 20;
if (perPage > 100) perPage = 100;                     // clamp the ceiling!
```

Defaults for missing values, a floor of 1, and a ceiling on `perPage` — without the clamp, `?perPage=1000000` lets any client ask your database for a million rows.

### Common mistakes

- Doing arithmetic on query values without parsing (`'2' + 1` → `'21'`).
- Forgetting `get` returns `null` for missing params — feed `?? ''` into parseInt rather than the literal string `'null'`.

lessons.title: Designing Resource URLs
lessons.explanation:
## Nouns, not verbs

REST URL design has one core move: model your data as **resources** (nouns), let the **method** carry the verb. The grid for one resource:

| intent            | method + route        |
|-------------------|-----------------------|
| list users        | `GET /users`        |
| read one          | `GET /users/42`     |
| create            | `POST /users`       |
| replace           | `PUT /users/42`     |
| partial update    | `PATCH /users/42`   |
| delete            | `DELETE /users/42`  |

Conventions that make APIs guessable:

- **Plural nouns** for collections: `/users`, not `/user`. The collection route and the item route share a prefix: `/users` and `/users/42`.
- **No verbs in paths.** `/getUsers`, `/users/42/delete` — the method already says it. A verb in the URL is usually a sign something is modeled wrong.
- **Nest for ownership, one level:** `/posts/10/comments` reads "comments OF post 10". Deeper nesting (`/users/1/posts/10/comments/5`) gets brittle — once a resource has its own ID, you can address it top-level: `/comments/5`.
- **Filters, sorting, paging live in the query string**, never in the path: `GET /users?role=admin&page=2`, not `/users/admins/page/2`.

### Worked example

```js
// "give me page 2 of the active projects of team 7, newest first"
GET /teams/7/projects?status=active&page=2&sort=-createdAt
```

Read it inside-out: the *path* pins down which collection (projects belonging to team 7); the *query* refines the view of it (filter, page, order). Identity in the path, options in the query — that split answers 90% of design questions.

### Common mistakes

- `POST /users/42` to update — POST on an ITEM route is nonstandard; use PUT/PATCH.
- Encoding filters into the path (`/users/active`) — now `/users/:id` and `/users/active` collide. (Is "active" an ID?)

lessons.title: JSON APIs: Envelopes & Safe Serialization
lessons.explanation:
## Consistent shapes in, consistent shapes out

A JSON API lives or dies on predictability. Two conventions carry most of the weight:

**1. Envelopes.** Successful responses wrap their payload: `{ "data": ... }`. Errors ALWAYS look the same: `{ "error": { "code": "NOT_FOUND", "message": "user 42 not found" } }`. One error shape means clients write ONE error handler. The `code` is a stable machine-readable token (screaming snake case by convention); the `message` is for humans and may change freely.

**2. Serialize deliberately.** Your database rows contain things clients must never see:

```js
const row = {
  id: 7,
  name: 'Ada',
  email: 'ada@x.io',
  passwordHash: '$2b$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMye...',   // NEVER ship this
  failedLogins: 3,                                      // internal
};

function userToPublic(u) {
  return { id: u.id, name: u.name, email: u.email };   // allow-list!
}
```

Walk through it: the public shape is built by **picking** the allowed fields, not by deleting the bad ones. An allow-list fails safe — when someone adds a `resetToken` column next sprint, it stays private by default. A deny-list (`delete u.passwordHash`) fails open: every new sensitive column leaks until someone remembers.

### Common mistakes

- Returning raw DB rows "temporarily". The leak always outlives the TODO comment.
- Error bodies that vary per endpoint (`{ msg }` here, `{ error: "string" }` there) — clients end up with a zoo of handlers.
- Forgetting `JSON.stringify` silently DROPS `undefined` values — a field can vanish from the wire without an error.

lessons.title: Validating Request Bodies
lessons.explanation:
## The gate every POST walks through

Never trust a request body. It comes from the network; it can be anything — missing fields, wrong types, 10-megabyte strings, extra fields you never asked for. Every write endpoint starts with the same move: **validate, and return 400 with specific errors before touching any data.**

The workhorse pattern is a **field spec**: a plain object describing each field, and a validator that compares the body against it, accumulating errors:

```js
const spec = {
  name:  { required: true,  type: 'string', maxLength: 50 },
  email: { required: true,  type: 'string', maxLength: 100 },
  age:   { required: false, type: 'number' },
};

validateBody({ name: 'Ada' }, spec)
// → [{ field: 'email', message: 'email is required' }]
validateBody({ name: 'Ada', email: 42 }, spec)
// → [{ field: 'email', message: 'email must be a string' }]
```

Walk through the first call: `name` passes all three checks; `email` is required and absent → one error; `age` is optional and absent → no error. Key behaviors: the validator returns **ALL errors at once** (a form wants every red field highlighted, not one per round trip), each error names its field, and an empty array means "proceed".

### Common mistakes

- Returning on the FIRST error. Accumulate instead — `errors.push(...)`, return the array.
- Treating `required` and type checks as one: an absent optional field is fine; a present-but-wrong-type field is not.
- Validating with truthiness: `if (!body.age)` rejects a legitimate age of `0`. Check `undefined`/type explicitly.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Which of these is NOT part of an HTTP *request*?
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Status codes belong to the response — they are the server's verdict on the request. A request carries a method, a path, headers, and (sometimes) a body; it cannot know its own outcome in advance.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: A client sends the header `Content-Type: application/json`. Your server stores headers lowercased. Is any information lost?
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: The HTTP spec says header names are case-insensitive, so `Content-Type`, `content-type`, and `CONTENT-TYPE` are the same header. Normalizing names to lowercase at the edge is exactly what real frameworks (including Node and Express) do. Header *values* keep their case — `application/json` stays as sent.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Your `req` object for an incoming `GET /users` request — what is in `req.body`?
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: GET requests ask for data; they do not send a payload. In our simulation that is `body: null`. (The users being fetched arrive in the *response* body — the request only names what it wants via the path.)

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: A request object is just an object: `req.method + ' ' + req.path` prints the request line (`POST /orders`), header lookup is plain bracket access with the lowercase name, and the parsed body is a normal object you can reach into (`req.body.qty` → 2).

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Responses mirror requests but swap method/path for a status code. `response.status` is the number 404, the body is a plain object (so `typeof` says `object`), and the error message is one property access away.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `makeRequest` that takes `(method, path)` and returns `{ method, path, headers: {}, body: null }`, with the method uppercased (e.g. `makeRequest('get', '/users')` → `{ method: 'GET', path: '/users', headers: {}, body: null }`).
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Normalizing the method to uppercase at construction time means every later comparison (`req.method === 'GET'`) is simple and safe. Fresh empty headers and a null body are the correct defaults for "no metadata, no payload yet".
hints: Return an object literal; call `.toUpperCase()` on the method.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `buildGet` that takes a path and returns a complete GET request object: `{ method: 'GET', path, headers: {}, body: null }`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Specialized builders like this read better at call sites than `makeRequest('GET', ...)` everywhere. A GET has no body by definition, so `body: null` is baked in rather than left to the caller.
hints: Hard-code the method; the path is the only variable part.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `buildPost` that takes `(path, body)` and returns `{ method: 'POST', path, headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body }` — a POST carrying JSON.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: When a request carries a body, the `content-type` header tells the server how to parse it. Forgetting it is a classic bug: the server sees bytes it does not know how to decode. Baking the header into the builder makes it impossible to forget.
hints: A POST that sends JSON must *say so* — set the 'content-type' header.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `requestSummary` that takes a request object and returns the string `'METHOD path'`, e.g. `'GET /users/42'`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: `'METHOD path'` is the standard one-line way to talk about a request — it is what access logs print and what you will write in every log middleware later. A template literal keeps it readable.
hints: Template literal with the two fields, separated by one space.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `withHeader` that takes `(req, name, value)` and returns a NEW request object with the header added under the lowercased name; existing headers are kept.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Two spreads build a new outer object AND a new headers object, so the original request is untouched — the immutable-update pattern from the objects course. The computed key `[name.toLowerCase()]` enforces the lowercase-names convention at the single point where headers enter.
hints: Spread the request, then spread its headers and add the new entry with a computed key.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `withBody` that takes `(req, body)` and returns a new request object with that body and the header `'content-type': 'application/json'` added (other fields and headers preserved).
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Body and content-type travel together: whenever you attach a JSON payload you must also declare it. Doing both in one helper keeps the invariant in one place instead of relying on every caller to remember.
hints: Same double-spread as withHeader, but set both the body and the content-type header.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `getHeader` that takes `(req, name)` and returns the header value, looking the name up case-insensitively (headers in `req.headers` are stored lowercase, but callers may ask with any casing). Return `null` when the header is absent. e.g. `getHeader(req, 'Content-Type')` finds `'content-type'`. Header names in `req.headers` are always stored lowercase.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Because headers were normalized to lowercase when stored, lookup only needs to lowercase the *asked* name. `?? null` converts the `undefined` of a missing property into an explicit `null`, which is easier for callers to test against.
hints: Lowercase the name before looking it up; `?? null` for the miss case.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `hasBody` that takes a request and returns `true` when `req.body` is neither `null` nor `undefined` (an empty object `{}` still counts as a body). Header names in `req.headers` are always stored lowercase.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: The check is about *presence*, not truthiness: `{}` is a real (if empty) payload, and a truthiness test would also wrongly reject a body of `0` or `""`. Comparing against null and undefined precisely captures "nothing was sent".
hints: Two strict checks — or the idiomatic `req.body != null`.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `isJsonRequest` that takes a request and returns `true` when its `content-type` header (lowercase key) *starts with* `'application/json'` — this must also accept `'application/json; charset=utf-8'`. Missing header → `false`. Header names in `req.headers` are always stored lowercase.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Content-type values often carry parameters after a semicolon (`; charset=utf-8`), so an equality check against 'application/json' is too strict — `startsWith` handles both forms. The `typeof` guard stops `undefined.startsWith` from throwing when the header is absent.
hints: Read the header, guard against it being missing, then `startsWith`.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `isWrite` that takes a request and returns `true` when its method is one of `'POST'`, `'PUT'`, `'PATCH'`, `'DELETE'` (the methods that change server state), else `false`. Header names in `req.headers` are always stored lowercase.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: An array + `.includes` beats a chain of `===` comparisons: the set of write methods reads as data, and adding one later is a one-token change. You will use exactly this check in middleware that, say, blocks writes for read-only users.
hints: Put the write methods in an array and use `.includes`.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export a function `pathSegments` that takes a request and returns its path split into non-empty segments, e.g. path `'/users/42/posts'` → `['users', '42', 'posts']`; path `'/'` → `[]`. Header names in `req.headers` are always stored lowercase.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: Splitting `'/users/42'` on `'/'` yields `['', 'users', '42']` — the leading slash creates an empty first piece. Filtering empties fixes that (and also handles trailing slashes). Routers are built on exactly this segment array, as you will see in the next course.
hints: Split on '/' — then throw away the empty strings the leading slash produces.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: Export `normalizeHeaders(raw)` that takes a headers object with arbitrary-case names and possibly-padded values and returns a new object with every name lowercased and every value trimmed. `{ "Content-Type": " application/json " }` → `{ "content-type": "application/json" }`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: This is the "normalize at the edge" function every server runs once per request, and the reason the rest of the codebase gets to assume lowercase names. Building a fresh object (instead of mutating the input) keeps the raw data available for debugging.
hints: Loop with `Object.entries`, writing into a fresh object.
Lowercase each key, trim each value.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: In the request `GET /users/42?fields=name`, which part is the `path` in our request objects?
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: The path identifies the resource: `/users/42`. The query string (`?fields=name` onward) is a separate component carrying options *about* the request — frameworks parse it into a separate `query` object, which a later lesson covers in depth.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: The first line of a raw HTTP request looks like `'GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1'`. Export `parseRequestLine(line)` that returns `{ method, path, version }` — e.g. `{ method: 'GET', path: '/users/42', version: 'HTTP/1.1' }`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: The request line is rigidly `METHOD SP PATH SP VERSION`, so one split plus array destructuring does the whole job. This is genuinely how the first line of every HTTP/1.1 request is parsed — the protocol was designed to be this easy to read.
hints: The three parts are separated by single spaces.
Destructure the result of `split(' ')` into three names.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions: A raw header line looks like `'Content-Type: application/json'`. Export `parseHeaderLine(line)` returning `{ name, value }` where `name` is lowercased and both parts are trimmed. Only split on the FIRST colon — values may contain colons (think `'Referer: https://x.io'`).
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: `'Referer: https://x.io'` contains two colons, so `split(':')` would shred the value. `indexOf` finds only the first colon; slicing around it keeps the value intact. Lowercasing the name (but not the value) applies the case-insensitivity rule exactly where it belongs.
hints: `split(':')` would break URLs in values — find the first colon's index instead.
`indexOf` + two `slice` calls, then trim both and lowercase the name.

bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.instructions:
Export `parseRawRequest(raw)`. The input is a raw HTTP request as one string:
the request line, then zero or more header lines, then a blank line, then the (possibly empty) body.
Lines are separated by `\n`, and the blank line separating headers from body is `\n\n`.

Return `{ method, path, headers, body }` where `headers` maps lowercased trimmed names to trimmed values, and `body` is the raw body string — or `null` when the body is empty.

Example: `'POST /users HTTP/1.1\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"name":"Ada"}'` →
`{ method: 'POST', path: '/users', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: '{"name":"Ada"}' }`
bootforge/http-rest/http/requests-and-re.explanation: This challenge composes the two parsers you just wrote. The key structural insight is the blank line: everything before it is metadata (one request line + header lines), everything after is opaque payload. Splitting at the FIRST `\n\n` matters because a body could itself contain blank lines. Mapping the empty string to `null` keeps the "no body" convention consistent with the rest of the course.
hints: First cut the string in two at the blank line: `indexOf('\n\n')`.
The head splits into lines: line 0 is the request line, the rest are header lines.
Reuse your parse-request-line and parse-header-line logic; empty body string becomes null.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: A payment request times out — you never saw the response. Which request is DANGEROUS to blindly retry?
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: POST is not idempotent: if the first request actually succeeded (the timeout hit on the way back), retrying creates a second payment. GET is safe, and PUT/DELETE are idempotent — repeating them converges to the same server state. This is why payment APIs require idempotency keys on POST.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: You want to change ONLY the email on a user record, leaving the other fields alone. Which method states that intent?
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: PATCH means "apply this partial modification"; PUT means "here is the complete replacement state". Sending only `{ email }` with PUT would, strictly, replace the whole user with a record that has nothing but an email. (And `UPDATE` is SQL, not HTTP — there is no such method.)

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Which set lists exactly the SAFE methods (no server state change)?
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Safe methods are the read-only ones: GET (read), HEAD (read headers only), OPTIONS (ask what is allowed). PUT and DELETE change state — they are idempotent, which is weaker than safe. Every safe method is idempotent, but not vice versa.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: You `DELETE /users/42`. It returns 204. You send the exact same request again and get 404. Was DELETE idempotent here?
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Idempotency promises the same resulting server state, not the same response. After one DELETE or five, user 42 does not exist — state identical. The 404 on the second call is just the server reporting "nothing here", which is accurate.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: A teammate adds `GET /users/42/delete` to the API — visiting the URL deletes the user. What is the strongest objection?
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: The whole web infrastructure assumes GET is harmless: link prefetchers, crawlers, and some proxies issue GETs freely. A state-changing GET WILL eventually be triggered by a machine. (This really happened: the Google Web Accelerator in 2005 followed "delete" links on web apps and wiped user data.) Use DELETE.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: The loop checks each of the five REST verbs against the idempotent set. POST and PATCH are the two that come out as DANGER — the two you must never blindly retry. This table is worth memorizing; everything else in this lesson derives from it.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Fetch a user profile to display it
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Reading data with no side effects is exactly what GET is for — safe and cacheable.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Save a document editor's "Save" button — the client sends the complete new document
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: The client has the full replacement state, so PUT /documents/:id is the honest verb: repeat-safe and total.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Change just the `done` flag on one todo, sending only that field
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: A partial modification — one field out of many — is PATCH. PUT would claim you are sending the whole todo.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Submit a brand-new order; the server will assign its ID
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Creation where the SERVER picks the identity is POST to the collection. (If the client chose the ID, PUT to that URL would also be defensible.)

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Remove a comment by its ID
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: DELETE /comments/:id says exactly what happens — and being idempotent, a nervous double-click does no extra harm.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Save a user's settings page — the client always sends ALL the settings, and saving twice should be harmless
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: "Full state, repeat-safe" is the definition of PUT. The double-save requirement rules out POST (not idempotent), and sending all fields rules out PATCH (partial).

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Which HTTP method fits this intent?

> Kick off a one-time CSV export job; each call should start a NEW job with its own ID
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Actions that create a new thing per call — jobs, emails, payments — are POST by nature: each invocation has a distinct effect, which is exactly what non-idempotent means.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export a function `isIdempotent(method)` that returns `true` for the idempotent methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE and `false` for POST and PATCH. Accept any casing (`'post'` → `false`).
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Normalizing case first means one clean membership check. Retry logic in HTTP clients does literally this: "is the method idempotent? then I may retry on timeout."
hints: Uppercase the input, then check membership in the idempotent set.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export a function `isSafe(method)` that returns `true` only for the safe (read-only) methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — any casing accepted.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Safe is a strictly smaller set than idempotent: PUT and DELETE mutate (not safe) but converge (idempotent). Caches use exactly this predicate — only safe requests are cacheable.
hints: Same shape as isIdempotent, smaller set.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export a function `canHaveBody(method)` that returns `true` for methods that conventionally carry a request body (POST, PUT, PATCH) and `false` for GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, DELETE — any casing.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: GET/DELETE bodies are technically possible but so unconventional that proxies and servers may drop them — APIs put inputs for those methods in the path and query string instead. The three state-sending verbs are where payloads belong.
hints: The body-carrying methods are the ones that send new state to the server.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export a function `needsIdempotencyKey(method)` that returns `true` exactly when the method is NOT idempotent (POST, PATCH, any casing) — those are the requests that need an idempotency key before being retried.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: An idempotency key is a client-generated unique ID sent with a POST so the server can detect "I already processed this exact attempt" on a retry. Only non-idempotent methods need the mechanism — the others are retry-safe by design.
hints: It is the complement of isIdempotent over the common methods.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export `chooseMethod(intent)` mapping an intent string to its HTTP method: `'read'` → `'GET'`, `'create'` → `'POST'`, `'replace'` → `'PUT'`, `'update'` → `'PATCH'`, `'delete'` → `'DELETE'`. Any other intent → `null`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: A plain object as a lookup table is the cleanest encoding of a fixed mapping: the data IS the logic. `map[intent] ?? null` handles the unknown-intent case in one token. Notice the five intents are precisely the five CRUD-ish verbs — this mapping is the skeleton of every REST API you will design.
hints: A lookup object beats an if/else chain.
Missing key gives `undefined` — turn it into `null` with `??`.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions: Export `describeMethod(method)` returning `{ safe, idempotent, hasBody }` (three booleans) for the method, any casing. Safe: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS. Idempotent: safe ones plus PUT/DELETE. hasBody: POST/PUT/PATCH. e.g. `describeMethod('put')` → `{ safe: false, idempotent: true, hasBody: true }`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: Each property is an independent membership test against its set — uppercasing once at the top avoids repeating `.toUpperCase()` three times. Returning the whole property card at once is how documentation generators and API linters model methods internally.
hints: Normalize the case once, then build the object from three membership checks.

bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.instructions:
Export `lintRequest(req)` that inspects a request object `{ method, path, body }` and returns an array of warning strings, in this order (include each only when its rule fires):

1. method not uppercase → `'method should be uppercase'`
2. (uppercased) method not one of GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE → `'unknown method'`
3. a SAFE method (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS, after uppercasing) with a non-null body → `'safe requests should not have a body'`
4. POST/PUT/PATCH (after uppercasing) with a null body → `'this method usually carries a body'`
5. path does not start with '/' → `'path should start with /'`

A clean request returns `[]`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/methods-and-sem.explanation: A linter is just a pipeline of independent predicates pushing messages into an accumulator — the same accumulate-errors shape you will reuse for request validation later in this course. Computing `upper` once serves two purposes: rule 1 detects casing by comparing original vs normalized, and every other rule works on the normalized form so `'yeet'` and `'YEET'` are judged the same.
hints: Build a warnings array and push into it; each rule is one `if`.
Uppercase the method once into a separate variable — rule 1 compares the original against it, rules 2-4 use it.
Order of the `if` statements determines order of the warnings — follow the prompt exactly.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.instructions: A logged-in regular user calls `DELETE /admin/users/7` and is not an admin. Which status?
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.explanation: The user IS authenticated (we know who they are) but lacks permission — that is 403 Forbidden. 401 would tell the client "authenticate and try again", which is wrong advice here: logging in again will not help.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.instructions: Your API moved from `/v1/users` to `/v2/users` forever, and you want clients and caches to remember that. Which redirect?
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.explanation: 301 is the permanent redirect — caches and clients may remember the new location and skip asking again. 302 says "temporarily elsewhere, keep using the old URL", and 304 is not a redirect at all (it means "your cached copy is still valid").

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.instructions: An endpoint returns `200 OK` with body `{ "error": "user not found" }`. What is the main problem?
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/qu.explanation: Everything between the two apps — caches, proxies, load balancers, dashboards, retry logic, `fetch` wrappers — reads the status code, not your body. A lying 200 means errors get cached, alerting stays green, and every client needs bespoke error-sniffing. The correct code here is 404.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/ou.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/ou.explanation: Integer-dividing by 100 isolates the first digit: 201→2, 404→4, 503→5, 301→3. The family carries the broad meaning (success / client error / server error / redirect) even for codes you have never met.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> POST /users succeeds and a new row was inserted. The response includes the new user.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 201 Created is the precise success code for "a new resource now exists". Plain 200 is not wrong, but 201 tells the client something 200 does not.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> DELETE /sessions/9 succeeds. There is nothing useful to put in the response body.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 204 No Content is success with an intentionally empty body — the standard answer for a successful DELETE.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> POST /users arrives with body { "email": 42 } — email must be a string.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: Malformed or invalid input is 400 Bad Request: the client can fix the request and try again. It is not a 500 — the server did nothing wrong.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> GET /me arrives with no Authorization header at all.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 401 Unauthorized (really: unauthenticated) — the server does not know who is asking. The response invites the client to authenticate and retry.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> An authenticated intern calls GET /payroll/all. Only HR may do that.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: Identity is known, permission is lacking: 403 Forbidden. Re-authenticating will not change the outcome, which is exactly what 403 signals.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> GET /users/999 — no user with id 999 exists.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 404 Not Found: the path was understood but names nothing that exists. (204 would claim success; 400 would blame the request's shape, which was fine.)

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> POST /users with an email that already belongs to another account.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 409 Conflict is for requests that are well-formed but collide with current server state — duplicate keys, version mismatches, already-processed transfers.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> A handler throws `TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined` and nothing catches it.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: An unhandled exception is a server-side bug: 500 Internal Server Error. The client sent a reasonable request and can do nothing differently.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> A client has sent 1,000 requests in a minute; your limit is 100.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is purpose-built for rate limiting, usually with a Retry-After header telling the client when to come back.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
What status code should this response carry?

> Your API is fine, but the database behind it is down for maintenance and nothing can be served.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: 503 Service Unavailable means "temporarily cannot serve — try later". It signals operational trouble rather than a code bug (500), and load balancers treat it as a health signal.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/ca.instructions: Export `categorize(code)` returning `'informational'` for 100-199, `'success'` for 200-299, `'redirect'` for 300-399, `'client-error'` for 400-499, `'server-error'` for 500-599, and `'unknown'` for anything else.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/ca.explanation: Dividing by 100 and flooring turns 404 into 4 — the family digit — and then a five-entry lookup object does the naming. This single function is why you never need to memorize individual codes to roughly understand a response.
hints: `Math.floor(code / 100)` gives you the first digit.
Map digit → name with a lookup object; `?? 'unknown'` for everything off the map.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/st.instructions:
Export `statusText(code)` returning the standard reason phrase for these codes, and `'Unknown'` for any other:
200 'OK', 201 'Created', 204 'No Content', 301 'Moved Permanently', 304 'Not Modified',
400 'Bad Request', 401 'Unauthorized', 403 'Forbidden', 404 'Not Found', 409 'Conflict',
429 'Too Many Requests', 500 'Internal Server Error', 503 'Service Unavailable'.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/st.explanation: Number keys in an object literal are coerced to strings and back transparently, so `texts[404]` just works. Typing this table out once is also the best memorization drill there is — these thirteen codes cover 99% of real API traffic.
hints: One lookup object, number keys are fine.
Finish with `?? 'Unknown'`.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.instructions: Export a function `isSuccess(code)` that returns `true` for codes 200-299 inclusive, else `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.explanation: Range checks beat listing codes: new 2xx codes you never anticipated still classify correctly. This is exactly what `fetch`'s `response.ok` does.
hints: A range check with two comparisons.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.instructions: Export a function `isClientError(code)` that returns `true` for codes 400-499 inclusive, else `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.explanation: Client errors mean "fix your request" — retrying unchanged is pointless. Distinguishing this family from 5xx drives real retry policies: 4xx → give up, 5xx → maybe retry.
hints: Same shape, 400s.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.instructions: Export a function `isServerError(code)` that returns `true` for codes 500-599 inclusive, else `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/is.explanation: Server errors are the family worth alerting on: the client did nothing wrong. Monitoring systems count exactly this predicate to compute error rates.
hints: Same shape, 500s.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.instructions:
Export `pickStatus(situation)` mapping a situation string to its status code:
'ok' → 200, 'created' → 201, 'no-content' → 204, 'bad-input' → 400, 'unauthenticated' → 401,
'forbidden' → 403, 'not-found' → 404, 'conflict' → 409, 'rate-limited' → 429, 'server-error' → 500.
Unknown situation → 500 (when in doubt, it's our bug).
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/pi.explanation: Defaulting the unknown case to 500 encodes a real principle: if the server cannot even classify what happened, that is by definition an internal error. Note which keys need quoting in the object literal — any key containing a dash.
hints: Lookup object again — keys with dashes need quotes.
The fallback is 500, not null: an unrecognized situation is itself a server-side surprise.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/sh.instructions: Export `shouldRetry(code)` — `true` only for statuses worth automatically retrying: 429, 502, 503, 504. Everything else (including 400, 401, 404, 500, and all 2xx) → `false`. (500 is debatable in real systems; for this exercise treat it as NOT retryable — a bug will not fix itself.)
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/sh.explanation: 429/502/503/504 all describe *transient* conditions — overload, a restarting upstream, a timeout — that genuinely may pass. 400/404 will fail identically forever, and a 500 usually means a bug that retries only amplify. Every production HTTP client has a function shaped exactly like this.
hints: The retryable set: rate limiting plus the "something behind the proxy hiccuped" trio.

bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/st.instructions:
Export `summarizeStatuses(codes)` that takes an array of status codes from an access log and returns a summary object:
`{ total, families, errorRate }` where
- `total` is the number of codes,
- `families` counts codes per family label ('2xx', '3xx', '4xx', '5xx' — only include families that occur),
- `errorRate` is the fraction of codes that are 400-599, rounded to 2 decimals with `Math.round(x * 100) / 100`.
Empty input → `{ total: 0, families: {}, errorRate: 0 }`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/status-codes/st.explanation: This is the count-into-an-object pattern applied to real ops work — every dashboard "requests by status family" panel is this loop. One pass collects both the family tally and the error count; the rate is computed once, at the end, and rounded only for presentation (the same round-at-the-edge discipline as money formatting).
hints: Guard the empty array first (division by zero → NaN).
The family label is `Math.floor(code / 100) + 'xx'`; count into an object with `?? 0`.
Count errors in the same loop; compute the rate once at the end.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: A client POSTs JSON and wants JSON back. Which header combination states that?
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Content-Type describes the body being sent (the request body, here); Accept expresses what the sender wants back. They answer different questions, so a JSON-in, JSON-out request carries both. (Body-Type and Response-Type do not exist.)

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Which is a correctly formed Bearer authorization header value?
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: The format is the scheme word `Bearer`, a single space, then the token — no colon inside the value (the colon separates the header NAME from the value: `Authorization: Bearer abc123`). A bare token with no scheme is also malformed; servers should reject it.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Cache-Control: no-store`?
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Despite the name, `no-cache` ALLOWS caching — it only forces a revalidation check with the server before each reuse. `no-store` is the strict one: nothing may be persisted (use it for sensitive data). The misleading naming makes this a favorite interview question.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Your server responds with a JSON body. Which header should the RESPONSE carry so the client parses it correctly?
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Content-Type always describes the body it travels WITH — on a response, that is the response body. Accept would be meaningless here (it expresses a wish about a future reply). Body-sniffing exists but is unreliable and a known security footgun; declare your type.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Why do production systems scrub the `Authorization` header from request logs?
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: A Bearer token IS the credential — possession equals authentication. A log file full of Authorization headers is a log file full of working logins for whoever reads it (including attackers who breach the logging system). Scrub it, along with cookies and API keys, before anything is persisted.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Splitting `'Bearer tok_42'` on the space yields exactly two parts: the scheme and the credentials. Destructuring those two positions is the entire mechanical core of Bearer parsing — the rest is validation.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `parseAuthHeader(value)` that parses an Authorization header VALUE like `'Bearer abc123'` into `{ scheme: 'Bearer', token: 'abc123' }`. Return `null` when the input is not a string, has no space, or either part is empty. Exactly one space separates the parts; extra parts mean malformed → `null`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Auth parsing must be strict: anything that is not exactly `scheme SP credentials` is attacker-adjacent input and should be rejected, not guessed at. Checking `parts.length !== 2` catches both the missing-space and the extra-space cases in one condition. Returning `null` (rather than throwing) lets the caller turn it into a clean 401.
hints: Guard the type first — headers can be absent.
Split on ' ' and insist on exactly two non-empty parts.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `extractBearerToken(headers)` that takes a headers object (lowercase keys) and returns the Bearer token from the `authorization` header, or `null` when the header is missing, the scheme is not exactly `'Bearer'`, or the token is empty. e.g. `{ authorization: 'Bearer t1' }` → `'t1'`; `{ authorization: 'Basic t1' }` → `null`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: This narrows the general parser to the one scheme your API accepts. Each early `return null` is one distinct failure mode (missing header, wrong scheme, empty token) and all of them will map to the same 401 later — the function answers only "is there a usable token?", keeping HTTP concerns out of it.
hints: Read `headers.authorization`, guard against absence.
Scheme must equal 'Bearer' exactly — a Basic header is not a bug, it's just not yours to handle.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `parseContentType(value)` splitting a Content-Type value into `{ mediaType, charset }`. `'application/json; charset=utf-8'` → `{ mediaType: 'application/json', charset: 'utf-8' }`; no charset parameter → `charset: null`. Trim whitespace around both parts; lowercase the media type.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Content-Type is a media type plus optional `;name=value` parameters. Splitting on the semicolon separates them; rest-destructuring collects however many parameters exist. Media types are case-insensitive (hence the lowercase), while charset values are conventionally left as-is. This parser is why `startsWith` hacks become unnecessary.
hints: Split on ';' — the media type is the first piece, parameters follow.
Each parameter is 'name=value'; you only care about charset.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `acceptsJson(acceptValue)` — given an Accept header value (comma-separated media types, possibly with `;q=` parameters), return `true` when the client accepts JSON: some entry's media type (the part before any `;`, trimmed) is `'application/json'` or `'*/*'`. A missing header (`null`/`undefined`) means the client accepts anything → `true`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: The absent-header default is the subtle part: per the HTTP spec, no Accept header means the client accepts anything. The pipeline split→map(strip params)→some(match) handles arbitrarily long accept lists, and `*/*` ("anything") must count as a JSON yes. Real content negotiation also ranks by q-values — the challenge below gets you closer.
hints: No Accept header means "no preference" — that is a yes.
Split on commas, strip each entry's ;q=... tail, then use .some().

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `parseCacheControl(value)` turning a Cache-Control value into an object: flag directives become `true`, `name=value` directives get their value (as a number when it is numeric). `'max-age=60, no-cache'` → `{ 'max-age': 60, 'no-cache': true }`. Trim whitespace; empty string → `{}`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Cache-Control is a tiny key/value language: flags (`no-cache`) and assignments (`max-age=60`). Representing flags as `true` and parsing numbers makes downstream questions trivial (`cc['max-age'] > 0`). The empty-string skip guards against trailing commas — parse defensively, format strictly.
hints: Split on commas, trim each directive, skip empties.
A directive either has an = (name/value) or not (boolean flag).
Convert numeric values with Number(), keeping non-numeric ones as strings.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export `maxAgeOf(headers)` — given a headers object (lowercase keys), return the numeric `max-age` value from the `cache-control` header, or `null` when the header is missing or carries no `max-age=<number>` directive. `{ 'cache-control': 'public, max-age=300' }` → `300`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Three distinct "no answer" cases (missing header, no max-age directive, non-numeric value) all collapse into `null`, giving callers one condition to test. Note `max-age=0` must come back as `0`, not null — another reason the guards check types and NaN rather than truthiness.
hints: Guard the missing header, then scan the comma-separated directives.
Find the one starting with 'max-age=' and Number() what follows.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export a function `hasHeader` that takes `(headers, name)` and returns `true` when the header exists — lookup is case-insensitive on `name` (stored keys are lowercase).
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: `in` tests key presence without caring about the value — important because a header can legitimately hold an empty string, which a truthiness check would misreport as 'absent'.
hints: The `in` operator checks key existence; lowercase the name first.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export a function `mergeHeaders` that takes `(base, extra)` — two header objects — and returns a NEW object with all entries from both; on a clash, `extra` wins.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Spread order IS the precedence rule: later spreads overwrite earlier keys. This one-liner is how API clients layer default headers under per-request overrides.
hints: Two spreads; the later one wins conflicts.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export a function `removeHeader` that takes `(headers, name)` and returns a NEW headers object without that header (name matched case-insensitively); the rest are kept.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: The computed-key + rest destructure (`{ [key]: _removed, ...rest }`) is the immutable "delete" idiom — no mutation, no `delete` operator. Proxies do this to strip hop-by-hop headers like `connection` before forwarding.
hints: Rest-destructuring with a computed key peels one property off immutably.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export a function `formatHeaders` that takes a headers object and returns the wire format: one `'name: value'` line per header, sorted by name alphabetically, joined with `'\n'`. Empty object → `''`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Object key order is technically insertion order, so sorting makes the output deterministic — vital for tests, caching keys, and request signing (AWS signature v4 sorts headers for exactly this reason).
hints: Object.entries → sort by key → map to "name: value" → join.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions: Export a function `withJsonHeaders` that takes a headers object and returns a new one with `'content-type': 'application/json'` and `'accept': 'application/json'` added (existing entries kept; these two overwrite on clash).
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: A JSON API client sets both directions in one helper: "I send JSON, I want JSON." Placing the literals after the spread makes them authoritative over whatever was there.
hints: Spread the input first so the JSON pair wins.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions:
Export `buildHeaders(options)` taking `{ json, token, maxAge }` (each optional) and returning a headers object:
- `json: true` → add `'content-type': 'application/json'`
- `token` (non-empty string) → add `'authorization': 'Bearer <token>'`
- `maxAge` (a number) → add `'cache-control': 'max-age=<maxAge>'`
Nothing requested → `{}`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: The maxAge case is the trap: `if (options.maxAge)` silently drops `max-age=0` (an explicitly-uncacheable directive!) because 0 is falsy. Checking `typeof === 'number'` honors every legitimate value. Options-object in, headers-object out is the standard shape for config builders.
hints: Start from an empty object and add conditionally — three independent ifs.
Careful with maxAge: 0 is a valid value, so test the TYPE, not truthiness.

bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.instructions:
Export `negotiate(acceptValue, available)`.
- `acceptValue`: an Accept header value — comma-separated entries, each optionally carrying `;q=...` parameters, e.g. `'text/html, application/json;q=0.9, */*;q=0.1'`.
- `available`: array of media types the server can produce, in the server's preference order.

Walk the client's entries IN ORDER (ignore q-values for ranking — client order wins):
- a concrete entry that appears in `available` → return it;
- a `'*/*'` entry → return `available[0]`;
- a partial wildcard like `'text/*'` → return the first available type whose prefix before the `/` matches.

No entry matches → return `null`. A `null`/`undefined`/empty `acceptValue` means "anything" → `available[0] ?? null`.
bootforge/http-rest/http/headers-and-con.explanation: Content negotiation is a double preference list: the client ranks what it wants, the server ranks what it has. Walking the client list outermost gives the client first say; wildcards defer to server preference (`available[0]`). Real negotiation also sorts by q-values before walking — the structure stays identical, only the ordering step is added. Express's `res.format()` and the `negotiator` npm package implement exactly this dance.
hints: First normalize: split on commas, strip ;q= tails, trim, drop empties.
Three kinds of entry: exact type, '*/*', and 'type/*' — handle each inside one loop over the client's list.
For 'text/*', compare the part before the slash against each available type's prefix.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: In `https://api.shop.io/products?color=red&page=2`, what is the query string?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Everything after the `?` is the query string: ampersand-separated `name=value` pairs carrying options. The path (`/products`) names the resource; the query refines the request (filtering, paging, sorting).

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: A request arrives with `?page=2`. What is `searchParams.get("page") + 1`?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Query values are ALWAYS strings. `'2' + 1` triggers string concatenation, giving `'21'` — the classic silent pagination bug. Parse first: `Number.parseInt(params.get('page'), 10) + 1` is `3`.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: You need `q=coffee mug&size=XL` in a URL. What is the correct, safe way to build it?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: If a VALUE contains `&` or `=` (a search for 'fish&chips'), naive concatenation corrupts the whole query string — the server sees extra parameters. `URLSearchParams` escapes every value correctly (space → `+`, `&` → `%26`) and decodes on the way back out.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `hostname` excludes the port (`host` would include it), `pathname` is just the path, and `searchParams.get` returns the decoded value — or `null` for a parameter that is not there. That trailing `null` is why defensive code writes `params.get(x) ?? fallback`.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `set` writes one value per name; `append` allows repeats — which is how multi-value params like `tag=sale&tag=new` exist. `toString()` percent-encodes everything (space becomes `+` in query strings), and `getAll` is the only way to see every value of a repeated name (`get` returns just the first).
hints: set replaces; append adds another entry under the same name. Spaces serialize as +.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `protocolOf(urlString)` that returns the protocol WITHOUT the trailing colon: `'https://x.io/a'` → `'https'`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: The URL class reports `'https:'` with the colon (matching the URL grammar). `slice(0, -1)` drops the last character; knowing this quirk saves everyone the `if (protocol === 'https')` bug that never fires.
hints: URL's .protocol includes the ':' — slice it off.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `hostnameOf(urlString)` that returns the hostname (no port): `'https://api.x.io:8080/a'` → `'api.x.io'`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `host` is `api.x.io:8080`, `hostname` is just `api.x.io`. Pick deliberately: certificate checks want hostname, connection pooling keys on host.
hints: hostname vs host: hostname excludes the port.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `pathOf(urlString)` that returns the pathname: `'https://x.io/users/42?f=1'` → `'/users/42'`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Even `https://x.io` has a pathname of `'/'` — the URL class normalizes it. Routers match against exactly this property, with the query already stripped.
hints: .pathname — note a bare domain still has pathname "/".

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `isSecure(urlString)` that returns `true` when the URL uses https: `'https://x.io'` → `true`, `'http://x.io'` → `false`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Comparing against `'https:'` (colon included) is the correct form; comparing to `'https'` silently never matches. Auth cookies and tokens should only ever travel over URLs where this returns true.
hints: Compare .protocol to 'https:' — WITH the colon.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `originOf(urlString)` that returns the origin (protocol + host, no path): `'https://api.x.io:8080/users?a=1'` → `'https://api.x.io:8080'`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Origin = scheme + host + port, the security boundary of the web: CORS, cookies, and postMessage all compare origins. The URL class computes it so you never assemble it by hand.
hints: .origin is precomputed for you.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `queryStringOf(urlString)` that returns the raw query string without the leading `?`, or `''` when there is none: `'https://x.io/a?p=1&q=2'` → `'p=1&q=2'`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `.search` is `'?p=1&q=2'` or the empty string; `.searchParams.toString()` would also work and re-encodes canonically. Either way you avoid `split('?')[1]`, which returns `undefined` (not `''`) for query-less URLs.
hints: .search includes the '?' (or is '' entirely) — strip the prefix.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `isValidUrl(urlString)` that returns `true` when the string parses as an absolute URL, `false` otherwise (hint: the `URL` constructor THROWS on invalid input): `'https://x.io'` → `true`, `'not a url'` → `false`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: The URL constructor is also a validator: it throws a TypeError on anything that is not an absolute URL (including bare paths like `/users/42`, which lack a scheme). try/catch converts throw-or-not into a clean boolean — a standard idiom.
hints: try/catch around the constructor.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export a function `fileNameOf(urlString)` that returns the last path segment: `'https://cdn.x.io/img/logo.png?v=2'` → `'logo.png'`; a path of just `'/'` → `''`. Use the `URL` class — no string surgery.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Working from `pathname` (not the raw string) means the query string and hash are already gone — `logo.png?v=2` is the bug this approach avoids. The last element after splitting a path ending in `/` is the empty string, which matches the spec here.
hints: Parse, take pathname, split on /, last element.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `getParam(urlString, name)` returning the (decoded) value of the query parameter, or `null` when absent. `getParam('https://x.io/s?q=coffee+mug', 'q')` → `'coffee mug'`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `get` both decodes (`coffee+mug` → `coffee mug`) and handles absence (returns `null`) — two chores you never want to hand-roll. Notice the returned `'2'` for page: still a string, as always.
hints: Parse the URL, then `.searchParams.get(name)` — it already returns null for misses.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `getAllParams(urlString, name)` returning ALL values of a repeated parameter as an array (empty array when absent). `'https://x.io/s?tag=a&tag=b'` with `'tag'` → `['a', 'b']`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Multi-select filters (`?tag=sale&tag=new`) arrive as repeated parameters. `get` would quietly hand you only `'sale'` — a bug that ships because it half-works. `getAll` returns every value, and an empty array (not null) when none exist, which iterates safely.
hints: `getAll`, not `get` — `get` silently returns only the first value.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `buildQuery(params)` that turns a flat object into an encoded query string (no leading `?`) using `URLSearchParams`. `{ q: 'coffee mug', page: 2 }` → `'q=coffee+mug&page=2'`. Keys keep the object's order. Empty object → `''`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: One constructor call encodes everything: spaces become `+`, and the second test shows the real payoff — an `&` or `=` INSIDE a key or value gets percent-escaped (`%26`, `%3D`) instead of corrupting the string's structure. Numbers are stringified automatically.
hints: URLSearchParams accepts a plain object directly; toString() does the encoding.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `addParam(urlString, name, value)` returning the full URL string with that query parameter set (replacing any existing value for the name). `addParam('https://x.io/users', 'page', '2')` → `'https://x.io/users?page=2'`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: The parse→mutate→serialize round trip is the safe way to edit URLs: the class keeps the `?` vs `&` bookkeeping, encoding, and ordering correct. `set` (replace) is what pagination links want — `append` would yield `?page=1&page=2`.
hints: Parse → set → toString. `set` replaces, `append` would duplicate.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `mergeQuery(urlString, params)` that sets every entry of the `params` object onto the URL's query (overwriting clashes, keeping other existing parameters) and returns the URL string. `mergeQuery('https://x.io/a?page=1&q=t', { page: '2', sort: 'name' })` → `'https://x.io/a?page=2&q=t&sort=name'`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: This is the engine behind "change one filter, keep the rest" UI links: existing parameters survive, overridden ones update in place, new ones append. Note the updated `page` stays FIRST in the output — `set` preserves the original position of a replaced parameter.
hints: Loop Object.entries(params), calling set for each.
set keeps the position of an existing param — new ones append at the end.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `hasParam(urlString, name)` → `true` when the query parameter exists at all, even with an empty value. `'https://x.io/s?q='` with `'q'` → `true`; `'https://x.io/s'` with `'q'` → `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `has` answers presence; `get` answers value. The difference shows with `?q=`: present with an empty value — `has` says true while `get` returns `''`. Some APIs treat a present-but-empty param differently from an absent one (e.g. `?fields=` meaning "no fields"), so the distinction earns its own method.
hints: `searchParams.has` — presence, not value.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `removeParam(urlString, name)` returning the URL string with that query parameter deleted (all its values); other parameters survive. A URL left with no parameters loses its `?` entirely.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: `delete` removes EVERY entry under the name (see the repeated `tag` case) and the URL class tidies up after itself — when the last parameter goes, so does the dangling `?`. Hand-rolled string surgery gets both of those wrong on the first try.
hints: Parse → searchParams.delete(name) → toString.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `resolveUrl(base, path)` using the two-argument `URL` constructor — `new URL(path, base)` — to resolve a (possibly relative) path against a base URL, returning the full string. `resolveUrl('https://api.x.io/v1/users', '/health')` → `'https://api.x.io/health'`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: The second constructor argument makes URL a resolver with browser-identical rules: a leading `/` replaces the whole path, a bare name appends to the directory, and an absolute URL ignores the base entirely (third case — a classic open-redirect gotcha to be aware of). API clients use this to combine a configured base URL with endpoint paths.
hints: The URL constructor takes (relativeOrAbsolute, base).

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions:
Export `parsePagination(queryString)` taking a raw query string (no `?`, may be `''`) and returning `{ page, perPage }` as NUMBERS:
- `page`: from the `page` param; default 1; anything non-numeric or < 1 → 1.
- `perPage`: from the `perPage` param; default 20; non-numeric or < 1 → 20; **clamped to at most 100**.
Parse with `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` via `new URLSearchParams(queryString)`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Every list endpoint you ever build runs this exact gauntlet: default the missing, floor the nonsense, cap the greedy. The `perPage` ceiling is a genuine security control — without it, `?perPage=10000000` is a one-line denial-of-service on your database. Parse, validate, clamp: in that order.
hints: get() can return null — feed `?? ''` into parseInt so you get NaN, not a crash.
Validate each number: NaN or below 1 falls back to the default.
The ceiling on perPage is separate from the default — clamp AFTER defaulting.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions: Export `parseSort(value)` for sort params in the `'-'`-prefix convention: `'name'` → `{ field: 'name', dir: 'asc' }`, `'-createdAt'` → `{ field: 'createdAt', dir: 'desc' }`. `null`, `undefined`, or `''` → `null`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: The `-prefix` convention (`?sort=-createdAt` for newest-first) is widespread — JSON:API standardized it. Converting the string into a `{ field, dir }` object at the edge means the sorting code deeper in never re-parses strings; it consumes structured data.
hints: Guard the empty cases first.
startsWith('-') decides the direction; slice(1) removes the prefix.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.instructions:
Export `buildListUrl(base, options)` where `base` is an absolute URL with no query string and `options` is `{ page, perPage, filters }` (all optional; `filters` is a flat object).
Build the URL's query in this exact order:
1. `page` — always present; default 1
2. `perPage` — always present; default 20, clamped to at most 100
3. each filter, in **alphabetical key order**, skipping entries whose value is `null`, `undefined`, or `''`
Return the full URL string.

Example: `buildListUrl('https://api.shop.io/products', { page: 2, filters: { color: 'red', brand: 'acme' } })` →
`'https://api.shop.io/products?page=2&perPage=20&brand=acme&color=red'`
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/urls-a.explanation: Deterministic ordering (fixed params first, filters alphabetized) makes URLs *canonical*: the same logical query always serializes identically, so caches hit, logs group, and tests compare equal. Skipping empty values keeps UI-generated URLs clean — a blank search box should not emit `q=`. This function is the mirror image of `parsePagination`: one builds what the other guards against.
hints: Destructure options with defaults: `const { page = 1, perPage = 20, filters = {} } = options;`
Set page and perPage first, then loop `Object.keys(filters).sort()`.
Skip null/undefined/empty-string filter values — but 0 would be legitimate.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Which route follows REST conventions for reading a single product?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Plural collection noun + item id: `/products/42`. The verb lives in the method (GET), not the path. The singular `/product/42` half-works but breaks the symmetry with the collection route `/products` — pick plural and stay consistent.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: A code review flags the route `POST /orders/42/cancel`. Under strict resource thinking, what is the most RESTful redesign?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Cancelling is a state change on the order — express it as data with PATCH, or as creating a cancellation sub-resource. DELETE would claim the order ceases to exist (it does not; cancelled orders still show in history), and GET must never mutate. (Pragmatic APIs do ship action routes — but know which rule you are bending.)

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Which URL best expresses "the comments of post 10"?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Both occur in good APIs: nesting (`/posts/10/comments`) makes the ownership relationship part of the resource identity; a top-level collection with a filter (`/comments?post=10`) scales better when comments are also addressed independently. `/posts/comments/10` is the one that means nothing — is 10 a post or a comment?

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: You find yourself writing `GET /users/1/posts/10/comments/5/reactions/9`. What is the standard advice?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Comment 5's identity does not depend on knowing it came via user 1 and post 10 — the extra path segments add places to be wrong (what if post 10 is not comment 5's post?) and force clients to carry context they may not have. One level of nesting for listing within a parent, flat routes for direct access.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Where do the "only admins, sorted by name, page 3" options belong for the users collection?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Views of a collection — filtering, sorting, paging — are query parameters on the collection route. Path segments would make every combination its own route and collide with `/users/:id` (is "admins" an id?). POST /search is a pragmatic escape hatch for giant queries, not the default.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Which method + route pair is conventionally WRONG?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: POST targets the collection to create a member; updates to an existing item are PUT (full) or PATCH (partial). `POST /users/42` is the odd one: the resource already exists, so "create" semantics do not apply.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: The URL for comment 5 of post 10 (nested style)?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Parent collection, parent id, child collection, child id — the nesting order mirrors ownership, and both nouns stay plural.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: The route to CREATE a comment on post 10?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: POST to the (nested) collection — the server will assign the new comment its ID. `/new` is a verb-ish leftover from server-rendered forms, not an API resource.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: List a user 7's unread notifications?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: The collection is `/users/7/notifications`; "unread" is a view of it, so it rides in the query string. A dedicated `/unread-notifications` route would multiply endlessly (unread? archived? flagged?).

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Where do most production APIs put their version?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Header-based versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json`) is the purist answer, but the path prefix won in practice: it is visible in logs, trivially routable, and impossible to forget. Either way, the point stands — breaking changes need SOME versioning seam, because you cannot update every client the day you deploy.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Your API needs "the currently authenticated user's own profile". Which route is the common convention?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: `/me` (or `/users/me`) is a singleton resource: the identity comes from the Authorization header, not the path. Making clients track their own id (option 4) works until the token is all they have — right after login. The alias also lets the server enforce 'you can only see yourself' naturally.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: A client sends `PATCH /health` but that route only supports GET. The most precise status code?
