bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: The PATH exists, the METHOD is not supported on it — that is exactly 405 Method Not Allowed (ideally with an `Allow: GET` header listing what works). 404 would lie about the resource existing; 400 would blame the request body.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `pluralizeResource(noun)` for route building: ends with `'y'` → replace with `'ies'` (`'category'` → `'categories'`); already ends with `'s'` → unchanged; otherwise append `'s'`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Yes, `'box'` → `'boxs'` is wrong English — deliberately. Real pluralizers (Rails' Inflector) carry hundreds of rules and still keep an exceptions table; route helpers settle for cheap-and-predictable because a route named `/boxs` is merely ugly, while an *unpredictable* route name breaks clients. Know where approximation is acceptable.
hints: Three cases, checked with endsWith; order matters — check the s-case first.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `actionRoute(action, resource, id)` returning `{ method, path }` for the five CRUD actions with a CONCRETE id substituted: `actionRoute('get', 'users', 42)` → `{ method: 'GET', path: '/users/42' }`; `'list'` and `'create'` ignore the id and target `'/users'`. Actions: list→GET collection, get→GET item, create→POST collection, update→PATCH item, remove→DELETE item. Unknown action → `null`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: This is `crudRoutes` one step closer to the wire: instead of the `:id` placeholder, the actual id is interpolated, producing something a client could send right now. API client libraries generate requests from exactly this kind of action table — the convention is so regular that the code writes itself.
hints: Same table as crudRoutes, but with the real id baked into the item path.
Build both paths once, then look the action up.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions:
Export `isConventionalRoute(path)` → `true` when a path follows the course conventions:
- starts with `'/'`
- every ODD-positioned segment (1st, 3rd, ... — the resource names) is all lowercase letters (a-z only)
- no segment equals one of the verbs `'get'`, `'create'`, `'update'`, `'delete'`, `'new'`, `'edit'`
- `'/'` alone is conventional.
`'/users/42/posts'` → `true`; `'/getUsers'` → `false` (uppercase); `'/users/42/edit'` → `false` (verb).
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Index parity does the heavy lifting again: positions 0, 2, 4... are resource names (held to naming rules), odd positions are ids (anything goes — `42`, `a1`, uuids). Encoding your team's conventions as an executable check like this — run in CI against the route table — is how conventions survive contact with deadlines.
hints: Split into non-empty segments; even INDEXES (0, 2, ...) are the resource positions.
Two checks per segment: the verb ban applies to all, the lowercase-letters rule only to resource positions.
The regex /^[a-z]+$/ tests "all lowercase letters".

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `routeFor(resource, id)` where `resource` is a plural noun: with only a resource → the collection route `'/users'`; with an id (string or number) → the item route `'/users/42'`. An id of `null`/`undefined` means collection.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: The null/undefined check (not truthiness!) matters because an id of `0` is legitimate and must produce `/users/0`, not the collection route. Client SDKs are full of this exact helper — it guarantees every call site builds paths the same way.
hints: Check the id against null AND undefined (or `id == null`).
Template literals assemble the path.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `nestedRoute(parent, parentId, child, childId)` building one-level-nested routes: `nestedRoute('posts', 10, 'comments')` → `'/posts/10/comments'`; with a `childId` → `'/posts/10/comments/5'`. `childId` of `null`/`undefined` means the child collection.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: The parent id is mandatory — a nested collection is meaningless without knowing WHOSE children you want — while the child id is optional exactly like in routeFor. Building the base once and appending keeps the two return paths from drifting apart.
hints: Build the three-segment base first, then conditionally append the child id.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `isItemRoute(path)` → `true` when the path addresses a single item, i.e. it has an EVEN number of non-empty segments (`'/users/42'` → 2 segments → `true`; `'/users'` → 1 → `false`; `'/posts/10/comments/5'` → 4 → `true`; `'/posts/10/comments'` → 3 → `false`). `'/'` (0 segments) → `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: In the strict `/collection/id/collection/id` convention, the segment count's parity tells you what kind of thing the path names. The `length > 0` guard keeps `/` (the root, zero segments — even!) from being misclassified as an item. Real routers are more flexible, but this parity rule is a great consistency linter for your own API.
hints: Split into non-empty segments first.
Conventional REST paths alternate collection/id — items have even length.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions:
Export `parseRoute(path)` that reads a conventional REST path as alternating collection/id pairs and returns an array of `{ resource, id }` — `id: null` when a trailing collection has none.
- `'/posts/10/comments/5'` → `[{ resource: 'posts', id: '10' }, { resource: 'comments', id: '5' }]`
- `'/posts/10/comments'` → `[{ resource: 'posts', id: '10' }, { resource: 'comments', id: null }]`
- `'/'` → `[]`
Ids stay strings.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Striding the segment array in steps of two converts the path grammar (collection, id, collection, id, ...) into structured data. `segments[i + 1] ?? null` gracefully handles the odd-length case where the final collection has no id. Keeping ids as strings is deliberate — path segments are text, and `'007'` must not silently become `7`.
hints: Split into non-empty segments, then walk them two at a time (`i += 2`).
The id partner may not exist for the last pair — `segments[i + 1] ?? null`.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions: Export `whereDoesItGo(kind)` returning `'path'` or `'query'` for a piece of request data: `'identity'` → `'path'`; `'filter'`, `'sort'`, `'pagination'`, `'search'` → `'query'`. Anything else → `'query'` (when unsure, the query string is the safe home).
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: The entire placement rule compresses to one comparison: identity (WHICH resource) goes in the path; everything describing HOW you want it (filtered, sorted, paged, searched) goes in the query. If you internalize one thing from this lesson, make it this function's one-liner.
hints: Only one kind of data earns a path segment.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.instructions:
Export `crudRoutes(resource)` (plural noun in, e.g. `'users'`) returning the five standard endpoints:
```
{
  list:   { method: 'GET',    path: '/users' },
  get:    { method: 'GET',    path: '/users/:id' },
  create: { method: 'POST',   path: '/users' },
  update: { method: 'PATCH',  path: '/users/:id' },
  remove: { method: 'DELETE', path: '/users/:id' },
}
```
The `:id` is a literal placeholder string (routers substitute it later).
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/rest-r.explanation: Five endpoints, two distinct paths — computing `collection` and `item` once makes the symmetry visible and typo-proof. This table IS the REST convention; code generators and frameworks like Rails produce exactly this mapping from a single resource name, and in the next course you will feed tables like this into a router.
hints: Compute the collection path and the item path once, then reference them five times.
Only list and create use the collection path.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Why do APIs wrap success payloads in `{ "data": ... }` instead of returning the bare array `[...]`?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: A bare array is a dead end: the day you need to return a total count alongside the items, you must break the shape. `{ data: [...] }` can grow `{ data, meta }` compatibly. (Bare top-level arrays also had a historical XSSI security issue in old browsers — one more reason the convention stuck.)

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Which strategy for keeping `passwordHash` out of API responses is safest long-term?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Deny-lists (delete the known-bad) fail open: the next sensitive column — resetToken, stripeCustomerId, internalNotes — leaks by default. An allow-list serializer fails closed: new columns stay private until someone consciously exposes them. "Sent to the client" means fully public; the frontend is not a security boundary.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: In `{ error: { code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "user 42 not found" } }`, why have BOTH `code` and `message`?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Clients write `if (body.error.code === "NOT_FOUND")` — that string is a contract and must never change. The message is documentation for a human reading logs or a UI fallback; improving its wording should never break a client. Branching on message text is the bug this convention prevents.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: `JSON.stringify` silently OMITS properties whose value is `undefined` (JSON has no such value), while `null` survives as `null`. After the round trip, `nickname` is gone entirely (`false`) but `lastLogin` is still present (`true`). APIs exploit this: set a field to undefined to drop it from the wire, null to explicitly send "empty".
hints: JSON has null but no undefined — stringify treats them very differently.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `ok(data)` returning the success envelope `{ data }`. `ok([1, 2])` → `{ data: [1, 2] }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Trivial on purpose: routing every success through one function is what makes the envelope *consistent*. `{ data }` is shorthand for `{ data: data }` — and note `null` is a valid payload (`{ data: null }`), distinct from having no data key at all.
hints: Shorthand property: `{ data }`.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `makeError(code, message)` returning `{ error: { code, message } }`. `makeError('NOT_FOUND', 'user 42 not found')` → `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'user 42 not found' } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: The twin of `ok` — every error, from every endpoint, flows through here, which is precisely how an API ends up with one error shape instead of twelve. The nesting under `error` lets clients distinguish success from failure with a single `if (body.error)`.
hints: Nest the two fields under an `error` key.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export a function `notFoundError(resource, id)` that builds the standard not-found error: `notFoundError('users', 42)` → `{ error: { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'users 42 not found' } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Parameterizing the resource and id keeps not-found messages uniform across every endpoint — grep-able in logs, predictable for clients. The code stays the same constant no matter which resource missed.
hints: Template literal for the message; the code is fixed.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export a function `validationError(fields)` that builds a validation error from an array of field names: `validationError(['name', 'email'])` → `{ error: { code: 'VALIDATION', message: 'invalid fields: name, email' } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: `join(', ')` formats one field or many with no special-casing. Real APIs often also include a structured `fields` array alongside the message — the human-readable summary plus machine-readable detail.
hints: join(', ') turns the array into the message tail.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export a function `unauthorizedError()` that takes no arguments and builds the fixed 401 body: `{ error: { code: 'UNAUTHORIZED', message: 'authentication required' } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Auth errors should be deliberately information-free: no hint whether the user exists, whether the token was close, or what went wrong internally. A fixed body is a security feature, not laziness.
hints: No parameters — the body is always identical.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export a function `conflictError(field, value)` that builds a duplicate-value conflict: `conflictError('email', 'a@x.io')` → `{ error: { code: 'CONFLICT', message: "email 'a@x.io' is already taken" } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: The 409-paired body tells the client exactly which field collided so the UI can highlight it. Quoting the value makes messages unambiguous even when the value contains spaces.
hints: Single quotes around the value inside the template literal.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `isErrorResponse(body)` → `true` when `body` is an object (not null) with an `error` property that is itself a non-null object. `{ error: { code: 'X', message: 'y' } }` → `true`; `{ data: [] }` → `false`; `null` → `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: The infamous `typeof null === 'object'` bug must be guarded at BOTH levels: the body itself and the error property. This predicate is what a client SDK runs on every response before deciding which path — resolve with data or reject with the error.
hints: Remember typeof null === 'object' — guard null explicitly, twice.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `pickFields(obj, fields)` returning a new object with only the listed fields — fields missing from `obj` are skipped entirely (not set to undefined). `pickFields({ a: 1, b: 2 }, ['a', 'z'])` → `{ a: 1 }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Iterating over `fields` (the allow-list) rather than the object is the structural difference between fail-closed and fail-open: unknown object properties can never sneak through. The `in` guard distinguishes "absent" from "present but undefined" — without it you would create keys the source never had.
hints: Loop the FIELD list, not the object — that is what makes it an allow-list.
The `in` check keeps absent fields truly absent.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `userToPublic(user)` returning ONLY `{ id, name, email }` from a full user row — whatever else the row contains (passwordHash, failedLogins, internal flags) must not appear.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Three explicit property reads, one new object: nothing else CAN leak, including the `resetToken` in the second test that did not exist when the function was written — that is the allow-list guarantee. Every resource in a real API gets a serializer exactly like this, usually in its own file.
hints: Build the new object from the three allowed fields — do not copy-then-delete.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `usersToPublic(users)` mapping an array of full user rows through the same `{ id, name, email }` projection. Empty array → empty array.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: List endpoints reuse the item serializer via `.map` — same projection, applied n times, so the collection can never leak what the item does not. The `({ ... })` parentheses around the arrow body are required; without them the braces parse as a function block.
hints: One `.map` with the projection arrow — parenthesize the returned object literal.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `redactFields(obj, fields)` returning a new object where each listed field that EXISTS in `obj` has its value replaced by `'[REDACTED]'`; other fields pass through, and listed-but-absent fields are not added. `redactFields({ user: 'ada', password: 'hunter2' }, ['password'])` → `{ user: 'ada', password: '[REDACTED]' }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Redaction differs from picking: logs want to show a field EXISTED (so you can debug "was a password sent?") without storing its value. Spread-then-overwrite keeps the operation non-destructive — the original object, still needed by the handler, is untouched. This pairs with the Authorization-scrubbing quiz from the headers lesson.
hints: Copy with spread, then overwrite the listed fields that exist.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `safeJsonParse(text)` that tries `JSON.parse` and returns `{ ok: true, value }` on success or `{ ok: false, error: 'invalid json' }` on any parse failure (never throws).
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Request bodies are attacker-controlled text, and `JSON.parse` throws on garbage — unhandled, that throw becomes a 500 where a 400 belongs. The `{ ok, value } | { ok, error }` result shape (a "result type") lets callers branch with an `if` instead of their own try/catch. Note `'null'` parses successfully to `null` — ok: true with a null value is not an error.
hints: try/catch around JSON.parse; return a result object from each branch.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Many JSON APIs send numeric database IDs as STRINGS (`"id": "9007199254740993"`). Why?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: JSON allows arbitrarily large number literals, but `JSON.parse` in JavaScript produces IEEE-754 doubles: 9007199254740993 parses as 9007199254740992. An off-by-one in an ID is a catastrophic, silent bug — Twitter hit exactly this with tweet IDs and added `id_str`. Sending IDs as strings sidesteps the whole class of problem.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `listEnvelope(items)` returning `{ data: items, meta: { count } }` where `count` is the array length. `listEnvelope(['a'])` → `{ data: ['a'], meta: { count: 1 } }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: The simplest useful `meta`: clients get the count without measuring the array, and the shape has room to grow (page, totalPages) without breaking anyone — the envelope payoff from the first quiz, in action.
hints: data plus a meta object carrying the length.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `metaFor(total, page, perPage)` returning `{ page, perPage, total, totalPages }` with `totalPages = Math.ceil(total / perPage)`. `metaFor(45, 2, 20)` → `{ page: 2, perPage: 20, total: 45, totalPages: 3 }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: `Math.ceil` is the right rounding because a partial page is still a page a user must be able to reach. The 0-total case falls out correctly (`ceil(0) === 0`). Extracting meta construction into its own function keeps the pagination challenge below honest — one source of truth for the math.
hints: Math.ceil — 45 items at 20 per page is 3 pages, not 2.25.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Export `stripEmptyFields(obj)` returning a new object without the properties whose value is `null` or `undefined` (other falsy values — `0`, `''`, `false` — stay). `{ a: 1, b: null, c: undefined, d: 0 }` → `{ a: 1, d: 0 }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: Sparse JSON ("only send what has a value") keeps payloads small and makes PATCH semantics clearer — an absent field means "do not touch", null would mean "clear it". The explicit two-value check (or the idiomatic `!= null`) protects `0`, `''`, and `false`, which are real data.
hints: Loop entries, copy everything except the two "empty" values.
The idiomatic single check is `value != null` (loose, on purpose).

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/json-a.explanation: The one-argument form produces the compact single-line wire format (no spaces at all). The third argument (indent = 2) pretty-prints across multiple lines — hence `true` — which is for logs and humans, never for responses: the extra whitespace is wasted bandwidth to a machine client.

This marries the envelope convention with the pagination math: `data` carries the window, `meta` tells the client where it stands (`totalPages` is what renders the page buttons). The 1-based→0-based conversion `(page - 1) * perPage` is THE off-by-one to internalize, and `slice`'s forgiving out-of-range behavior turns the overshoot case into a non-event. Combined with `parsePagination` from earlier, you now have both halves of every list endpoint.
hints: The start index is `(page - 1) * perPage` — page numbers are 1-based, indexes 0-based.
`slice` past the end returns `[]` with no error, which handles the overshoot case for free.
`Math.ceil(0 / perPage)` is already 0 — no special case needed.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: A signup form POSTs a body with three invalid fields. What should the 400 response contain?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Fail-fast is for programmers; forms are for humans. Returning one error at a time forces the user through submit→fix→submit loops, discovering one problem per trip. Accumulating errors (each with a field name) lets the UI light up every invalid input at once.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: The frontend already validates the form in JavaScript. Why must the server validate again?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The browser is the polite client. `curl -X POST api.x.io/users -d '{"role":"admin"}'` never ran your React validators. Client-side validation is UX (instant feedback); server-side validation is security and data integrity. You need both, and only one of them is optional.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Your validator uses `if (!body.quantity) errors.push("quantity is required")`. A customer orders with `quantity: 0`... wait, but also `quantity: 2` works. What orders break?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: `!0` is `true`, so `quantity: 0` fails the 'required' check despite being present. The falsy family — 0, '', false, NaN — are all legitimate VALUES a client may send. Required means 'not undefined' (`body.quantity === undefined`), nothing more.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: `typeof` is the validator's main tool: strings and booleans report themselves, an absent property reports `'undefined'`. The sting is in line 4: the client sent age as the STRING `'36'`, so a strict comparison against the number 36 is false — exactly the kind of type mismatch `type: 'number'` specs exist to catch.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Some APIs answer invalid bodies with 400, others with 422 Unprocessable Entity. What is the practical guidance?
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The distinction (unparseable vs parseable-but-wrong) is real but subtle, and clients mostly just check "is it 4xx with an error body". What actually hurts clients is inconsistency — validation failing with 400 on one endpoint and 422 on another. This course standardizes on 400.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `isNonEmptyString(v)` → `true` only when `v` is a string whose trimmed length is > 0. `'  hi '` → `true`; `'   '` → `false`; `42` → `false`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The && short-circuit is load-bearing: when `v` is 42, the right side never runs, so `.trim()` cannot throw. Whitespace-only strings counting as empty matches what users mean — a name of three spaces is not a name. This predicate appears in virtually every validator you will write.
hints: Type check first (so .trim() cannot crash), then trimmed length.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `normalizeStrings(body)` returning a new object where every string value is trimmed; non-string values pass through unchanged. `{ name: "  Ada ", age: 36 }` → `{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Normalization runs BEFORE validation in a typical pipeline, so `"  "` correctly fails a required-name check and `" a@x.io "` does not get stored with padding (which would break login later — `"a@x.io" !== " a@x.io"`). The typeof guard keeps numbers and booleans from being coerced.
hints: Loop entries; a ternary applies trim only to strings.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Query values are strings, so booleans arrive as text. Export `parseBoolParam(value)`: `'true'` → `true`, `'false'` → `false`, anything else (including `null`, `'1'`, `'TRUE'`) → `null` (meaning "not provided / invalid").
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Three-state results matter for filters: `?done=true` filters to done, `?done=false` filters to not-done, and no param at all means "don't filter" — collapsing the third state into `false` would make those last two indistinguishable. Being strict (rejecting `'TRUE'`, `'1'`) keeps the API contract documentable.
hints: Exact string comparisons; everything else is null.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Path params are strings too. Export `validateIdParam(raw)` — parse with `Number.parseInt(raw, 10)`; when the result is an integer ≥ 1 AND the raw string is exactly its decimal form (so `'7x'` and `'07'` fail), return `{ ok: true, id: <number> }`; otherwise `{ ok: false, error: 'invalid id' }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: `parseInt`'s leniency is a liability for IDs: `'7x'` → 7 would make `/users/7x` silently serve user 7, and `'07'` vs `'7'` would be two URLs for one resource (bad for caching and security filters). The round-trip comparison `String(parsed) === raw` is a compact way to demand canonical form. The `{ ok, ... }` result feeds a 400-or-continue branch in the handler.
hints: parseInt is permissive — '7x' parses to 7, '07' to 7.
The round-trip check `String(id) === raw` rejects anything that was not a clean decimal.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `errorsByField(errors)` — given an array of `{ field, message }` objects, return an object mapping each field to the array of its messages, in order. `[{ field: 'a', message: 'm1' }, { field: 'a', message: 'm2' }, { field: 'b', message: 'm3' }]` → `{ a: ['m1', 'm2'], b: ['m3'] }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The flat error array is ideal for producing; the grouped shape is ideal for consuming — a form component asks "errors for THIS input?" with one property access. Group-by (initialize-on-first-sight, then push) is the same pattern as the status-family counter, producing arrays instead of counts.
hints: The group-by pattern: create the array on first sight of a key, then push.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `missingFields(body, required)` — given a body object and an array of required field names, return the names that are `undefined` in the body (in the order of the `required` list). Present-but-falsy values (0, '', false, null) are NOT missing.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: One `filter` with `=== undefined` implements "required" correctly: `0`, `''`, `false`, and even `null` are present values (whether null is *valid* is a separate, type-level question). Filtering the `required` list also gives you deterministic error ordering for free.
hints: Filter the required list by a strict undefined check.
Explicitly `=== undefined` — NOT truthiness.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions:
Export `typeErrors(body, types)` where `types` maps field names to expected typeof strings (e.g. `{ age: 'number', name: 'string' }`).
For each spec'd field that is PRESENT (not undefined) but whose `typeof` differs, produce the message `'<field> must be a <type>'`.
Absent fields produce nothing (required-ness is someone else's job). Return the array of messages in spec order.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Separating concerns makes validators composable: this function answers only "of the fields that showed up, are they the right type?" An absent optional field is silently fine here, and an absent *required* field is `missingFields`'s problem. The two layers combine cleanly in the challenge.
hints: Object.entries(types) gives [field, expectedType] pairs.
Skip undefined values — absent is not a TYPE error.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `tooLong(body, maxLengths)` where `maxLengths` maps field names to limits (e.g. `{ name: 50 }`). For each spec'd field present as a string whose `.length` exceeds the limit, produce `'<field> must be at most <n> characters'`. Non-string or absent values produce nothing. Return messages in spec order.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Length limits are not pedantry: they protect your database column sizes and stop the 10MB-string memory attack. Checking `typeof value === 'string'` first means a numeric value does not crash on `.length` — the type layer will flag it instead. Each validator stays in its lane.
hints: Only strings have meaningful lengths here — guard with typeof first.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `validateEnum(value, field, allowed)` — when `value` is undefined or appears in the `allowed` array, return `null`; otherwise return the message `'<field> must be one of: a, b, c'` (the allowed values joined with `', '`).
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Enums ("one of these exact values") guard status fields, roles, and sort directions. The subtle line: `undefined` means the field was omitted (fine — required-ness is separate), but `null` was actively SENT and is not an allowed value, so it fails. Echoing the allowed list in the message turns the error into documentation.
hints: undefined (absent) passes; anything else must be in the list.
Note null does NOT pass — it is a present value that is not in the list.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `validateRange(value, field, min, max)` — `null` when `value` is undefined, or is a number within `[min, max]` inclusive. `'<field> must be a number'` when present but not a number (NaN counts as not a number). `'<field> must be between <min> and <max>'` when a number out of range.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The gate ORDER is the design: you cannot range-check a string, so the type gate must come first, and `NaN` (which typeof calls a number but which fails every comparison) must be caught with it. Inclusive bounds (`<` and `>`, not `<=`/`>=`) match the "between 1 and 10" phrasing — both endpoints valid.
hints: Three gates in order: absent → fine; wrong type → type message; out of range → range message.
typeof NaN is 'number' — add the Number.isNaN check.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export `cleanBody(body, allowedFields)` returning a new object containing only the allowed fields that are present (not undefined) in the body — the mass-assignment defense. `cleanBody({ name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }, ['name', 'email'])` → `{ name: 'Ada' }`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: This is `pickFields` pointed at the INPUT side, and it closes a real vulnerability: mass assignment. If your update handler does `Object.assign(user, body)`, a client adding `"isAdmin": true` to the JSON promotes themselves — unless unknown fields were stripped first. GitHub was famously hit by exactly this in 2012.
hints: Same allow-list loop as pickFields — applied to input instead of output.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export a function `validateNewTodo(body)` that validates a new-todo body against: `title` required, string, maxLength 100; `done` optional, boolean. Error messages, in check order: `'title is required'`, `'title must be a string'`, `'title must be at most 100 characters'`, `'done must be a boolean'`. Return ALL applicable errors as an array of strings; a valid body returns `[]`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The else-if ladder per field reports the FIRST applicable problem only — "title is required" and "title must be a string" can never both fire, which keeps messages sensible. Optional fields skip the required rung and start at the type check, guarded by `!== undefined`.
hints: Per field: an if/else-if ladder (required → type → length), pushing at most one error per field.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export a function `validateLogin(body)` that validates a login body: `email` required, string, must contain `'@'`; `password` required, string. Messages in check order: `'email is required'`, `'email must be a string'`, `'email must contain @'`, `'password is required'`, `'password must be a string'`. Return ALL applicable errors as an array of strings; a valid body returns `[]`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: The `@` check is deliberately crude — real email validation is famously impossible with simple rules, and the pragmatic standard is 'contains @, then send a confirmation email'. The structure to notice: each field's ladder is independent, so both fields can report errors in one pass.
hints: Two independent ladders; the email one has a third rung for the @ check.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions: Export a function `validateNewUser(body)` that validates a new-user body: `name` required, string, maxLength 50; `email` required, string, must contain `'@'`; `age` optional, number, between 13 and 120 inclusive. Messages in check order: `'name is required'` / `'name must be a string'` / `'name must be at most 50 characters'`, then email's (`'email is required'` / `'email must be a string'` / `'email must contain @'`), then `'age must be a number'` / `'age must be between 13 and 120'`. Return ALL applicable errors as an array of strings; a valid body returns `[]`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: Three fields, three independent ladders, one accumulated array — the full shape of a production validator in miniature. The optional `age` wraps its whole ladder in a presence check, so omitting it is fine but sending nonsense is not. After writing this by hand, schema libraries like zod will feel like well-earned sugar.
hints: Three ladders: two required fields, one optional (wrap it in `if (body.age !== undefined)`).

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions:
Export `validateBody(body, specs)` — the generic engine behind every validator above.
`specs` maps field names to `{ required, type, maxLength }` (each key optional).
For each field IN SPEC ORDER, apply this ladder and record at most one error per field as `{ field, message }`:

1. `required: true` and the value is `undefined` → `'<field> is required'` (an absent optional field: skip remaining checks, no error)
2. value present and `type` given and `typeof value !== type` → `'<field> must be a <type>'`
3. value present, is a string, `maxLength` given, and longer → `'<field> must be at most <n> characters'`

Valid body → `[]`.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: This is the generalization the three hand-written validators were building toward: the SPEC is data, the engine is generic, and adding a field to an endpoint means editing an object literal, not writing new code. The `continue` statements encode "at most one error per field": each field exits the ladder at its first failure. Structured `{ field, message }` errors (rather than strings) are what lets a frontend attach each message to its input. This engine, grown up, is zod/Joi/ajv — and now you know what they do inside.
hints: Loop Object.entries(specs); for each field run the ladder and `continue` after recording an error.
Handle the undefined case first — it either errors (required) or skips (optional), but never falls through to type checks.
Return `{ field, message }` objects, not bare strings.

bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.instructions:
Tie the whole lesson together. Export `processRegistration(body)` that:
1. Validates: `name` required string (max 50); `email` required string containing `'@'`; `role` optional, one of `'user'` or `'admin'`.
   Messages (check order per field, at most one each): `'name is required'` / `'name must be a string'` / `'name must be at most 50 characters'`; `'email is required'` / `'email must be a string'` / `'email must contain @'`; `'role must be one of: user, admin'`.
2. Invalid → return `{ ok: false, errors }` (the string array).
3. Valid → return `{ ok: true, user: { name, email, role } }` where `role` defaults to `'user'` and name/email are TRIMMED. Unknown body fields must not appear.
bootforge/http-rest/rest-and-urls/reques.explanation: This is the shape of every production POST handler: validate everything, bail with ALL the errors, then construct the stored object explicitly — validated, trimmed, defaulted, and allow-listed in a single literal. Order matters: trimming before type-checking would crash on a numeric name, so normalization happens only after validation proves the types. The `{ ok, ... }` result keeps the function pure and testable; the next course turns results like this into 400/201 responses.
hints: Validate first (accumulate), return early on errors, only THEN build the clean user.
Building `user` from named fields IS the clean-body step — `isAdmin: true` never gets a chance.
Default the role with `?? 'user'` and trim at the end, when you know the values are strings.
